::: {.callout-tip}
This page covers programming basics with examples in R and Python. Every code block is **interactive**: edit the code and press **Run Code** to see what changes. We encourage you to play around!

You can click to switch between languaged. Picking **R** or **Python** in one tabset switches every tabset on the page. Callouts marked **R vs Python** point out the places where the two languages behave differently in notable ways.
:::

## Basics

The most common way you will interact with R and Python is through a **REPL** (read-evaluate-print-loop):

- You type out one or more statements (instructions)
- You ask the language *interpreter* to *execute* (evaluate) them
- It returns (prints) any output
- Repeat

Run the code cell below to see the output of `1+1`

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{webr}
# This is a comment R will ignore
# Try changing the statement below and rerun the code to see what happens
1 + 1
```

## Python

```{pyodide}
# This is a comment Python will ignore
# Try changing the statement below and rerun the code to see what happens
1 + 1
```

:::

## Values, variables, and types

To do more than simple calculations we need to *store* inputs and outputs (**values**). To do this we declare **variables**, which can hold different **types** of values.

### Text

To store text we wrap it in single `''` or double `""` quotes to create a **string**:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
# We assign variables using <-
my_string <- "hello psyc 201"

# Typing a variable by itself prints its value
my_string
```

## Python

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: true
# We assign variables using =
my_string = "hello psyc 201"

# Typing a variable by itself prints its value
my_string
```

:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## R vs Python: assignment
R assigns with `<-` (it also accepts `=`). Python only uses `=`. In both languages a single `=` **assigns** a value and a double `==` **compares** two values.
:::

### Numbers

We typically work with two kinds of numbers: *integers* (whole numbers) and *floats* (numbers with decimals):

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
my_number <- 3
my_decimal <- 3.1

# class() tells us what type a value is
class(my_number)
```

```{webr}
class(my_decimal)
````

## Python

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: true
my_number = 3
my_decimal = 3.1

# type() tells us what type a value is
type(my_number)
```

```{pyodide}
type(my_decimal)
```

:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## R vs Python: integers and floats
R treats both `3` and `3.1` as `numeric` unless you ask for an integer with `3L`. Python keeps `int` and `float` separate, but mixing them is safe as Python will convert to higher precision floats for you.
:::

### Booleans

Booleans store whether something is *true* or *false*:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{webr}
is_sunny <- TRUE
is_raining <- FALSE

class(is_sunny)
```

## Python

```{pyodide}
is_sunny = True
is_raining = False

type(is_sunny)
```

:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## R vs Python: spelling booleans
R writes `TRUE` and `FALSE`. Python writes `True` and `False`. Typing `TRUE` in Python gives a `NameError` because Python thinks you are referring to a variable you never defined.
:::

### Comparisons

Comparing values produces booleans. We combine comparisons with *and*, *or*, and *not*:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{webr}
my_decimal > my_number
```

```{webr}
# Not equal
my_decimal != my_number
```

```{webr}
# Combine with & (and), | (or), and ! (not)
my_number > 2 & my_number < 10
```

```{webr}
my_number > 100 | my_number < 5
```

```{webr}
!(my_number == 3)
```

## Python

```{pyodide}
my_decimal > my_number
```

```{pyodide}
# Not equal
my_decimal != my_number
```

```{pyodide}
# Combine with and, or, and not
my_number > 2 and my_number < 10
```

```{pyodide}
my_number > 100 or my_number < 5
```

```{pyodide}
not (my_number == 3)
```

:::

What happens when we compare a number to a string?

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{webr}
#| error: true
# R silently converts the number to text and compares alphabetically
my_number > my_string
```

```{webr}
#| error: true
# R also converts numbers to text for you when pasting strings together
paste("age:", 25)
```

## Python

```{pyodide}
#| error: true
# Python refuses to compare a number to a string
my_number > my_string
```

```{pyodide}
#| error: true
# Python also refuses to glue a string to a number
"age: " + 25
```

:::

::: {.callout-important}
## R vs Python: converting between types
R quietly converts types for you when it can. Python never does, and raises a `TypeError` instead. To mix types in Python, convert them yourself with `str()`, `int()`, or `float()`:

```{pyodide}
"age: " + str(25)
```

Python's strictness is a feature. Silent conversion is a common source of bugs in data analysis.
:::

## Containers

Most data analysis involves *many* values at once. Both languages have a container for an ordered sequence of values:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
# A vector, created with c()
fruits <- c("apple", "banana", "cherry", "date")
fruits
```

```{webr}
# length() tells us how many items it holds
length(fruits)
```

## Python

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: true
# A list, created with []
fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry", "date"]
fruits
```

```{pyodide}
# len() tells us how many items it holds
len(fruits)
```

:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Vectors vs lists
An R vector holds values of a single type (all numbers, or all strings). A Python list can mix types, so `[1, "two", 3.0]` is allowed. In practice you will rarely want a mixed list.
:::

### Indexing and slicing

To pull out individual items we **index** with square brackets. To pull out a range of items we **slice**:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{webr}
# First item (R starts counting at 1)
fruits[1]
```

```{webr}
# Last item
fruits[length(fruits)]
```

```{webr}
# Items 1 through 2 (both ends included)
fruits[1:2]
```

```{webr}
# Everything except the first item
fruits[-1]
```

## Python

```{pyodide}
# First item (Python starts counting at 0)
fruits[0]
```

```{pyodide}
# Last item (negative numbers count from the end)
fruits[-1]
```

```{pyodide}
# Items 0 up to but NOT including 2
fruits[0:2]
```

```{pyodide}
# Leave off start or stop to mean "from the beginning" or "to the end"
fruits[1:]
```

:::

::: {.callout-important}
## R vs Python: counting from 0 or 1
This is the first big difference to get used to. **R counts from 1, Python counts from 0**, and Python slices exclude the stop position. The rule applies everywhere: the first row of a Python dataframe is row 0.

| What you want | R | Python |
|---------------|---|--------|
| First item | `x[1]` | `x[0]` |
| First 3 items | `x[1:3]` | `x[0:3]` or `x[:3]` |
| Last item | `x[length(x)]` or `tail(x, 1)` | `x[-1]` |

Negative numbers also mean different things. In R `x[-1]` *removes* the first item. In Python `x[-1]` *returns* the last item.
:::

### Adding items

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{webr}
# c() builds a new, longer vector, so we assign it back to fruits
fruits <- c(fruits, "elderberry")
fruits
```

## Python

```{pyodide}
# .append() changes the list in place. Notice it prints nothing
fruits.append("elderberry")
```

```{pyodide}
fruits
```

:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## R vs Python: `.append()` returns nothing
In R you get a new vector back and assign it. In Python `.append()` modifies the existing list and returns `None`. Never write `fruits = fruits.append("fig")`, which overwrites your list with `None`. Call `fruits.append("fig")` on its own line instead.
:::

### Named collections

Sometimes we want to look values up by *name* instead of position. Think of these as **one row of a dataframe**: each name is a column and each value is that row's entry:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{webr}
# A named list
participant <- list(id = "p01", age = 22, condition = "easy")

# Look up by name with $
participant$age
```

```{webr}
# Add a new entry
participant$score <- 0.85
str(participant)
```

## Python

```{pyodide}
# A dictionary (dict) of key: value pairs
participant = {"id": "p01", "age": 22, "condition": "easy"}

# Look up by key with []
participant["age"]
```

```{pyodide}
# Add a new entry
participant["score"] = 0.85
participant
```

:::

## Control flow

So far every line has run once, top to bottom. **Control flow** lets us make decisions and repeat work.

### Conditionals

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{webr}
score <- 85

if (score >= 90) {
  print("A")
} else if (score >= 80) {
  print("B")
} else {
  print("C or below")
}
```

## Python

```{pyodide}
score = 85

if score >= 90:
    print("A")
elif score >= 80:
    print("B")
else:
    print("C or below")
```

:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## R vs Python: braces vs indentation
R uses `{ }` to mark which lines belong to an `if` or `for`. Python uses a `:` followed by **indentation**, and the indentation is not optional. Forgetting to indent gives an `IndentationError`:

```{pyodide}
#| error: true
if score > 50:
print("passing")
```

Most editors indent for you, so you will usually hit this error when editing existing code.
:::

### Loops

A `for` loop runs the same block of code once for each item in a collection:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{webr}
for (fruit in fruits) {
  print(fruit)
}
```

```{webr}
# Loop over a range of numbers
for (i in 1:3) {
  print(i ** 2)
}
```

```{webr}
# Loop over positions AND items
for (i in seq_along(fruits)) {
  print(paste(i, fruits[i]))
}
```

## Python

```{pyodide}
for fruit in fruits:
    print(fruit)
```

```{pyodide}
# Loop over a range of numbers
for i in range(3):
    print(i ** 2)
```

```{pyodide}
# Loop over positions AND items
for i, fruit in enumerate(fruits):
    print(i, fruit)
```

:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## R vs Python: `1:3` vs `range(3)`
R's `1:3` gives `1, 2, 3`. Python's `range(3)` gives `0, 1, 2`. Like slicing, it starts at 0 and stops before 3. To get `1, 2, 3` in Python write `range(1, 4)`.
:::

## Functions and methods

A **function** packages up a block of code so you can reuse it. You have been calling built-in functions all along (`print()`, `length()`, `len()`). Here is how to write your own:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
calculate_mean <- function(values) {
  total <- sum(values)
  n <- length(values)
  return(total / n)
}

calculate_mean(c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5))
```

```{webr}
# Arguments can have default values
greet <- function(name, greeting = "Hello") {
  paste0(greeting, ", ", name, "!")
}

greet("Alex")
greet("Alex", greeting = "Hi")
```

## Python

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: true
def calculate_mean(values):
    total = sum(values)
    n = len(values)
    return total / n

calculate_mean([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
```

```{pyodide}
# Arguments can have default values
def greet(name, greeting="Hello"):
    return f"{greeting}, {name}!"

print(greet("Alex"))
print(greet("Alex", greeting="Hi"))
```

:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## R vs Python: defining functions
R uses the `function` keyword and braces. Python uses `def`, a colon, and indentation. R returns the last expression automatically, so `return()` is optional. Python only returns what you explicitly `return`.
:::

### Methods

Python attaches some functions directly to values. These are **methods**, and you call them with a `.`:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{webr}
# R uses plain functions
toupper(my_string)
```

```{webr}
# Chaining steps with the pipe |>
my_string |> toupper() |> tolower()
```

## Python

```{pyodide}
# Python strings have an .upper() method
my_string.upper()
```

```{pyodide}
# Chaining steps with .
my_string.upper().lower()
```

:::

::: {.callout-note}
## R vs Python: methods and chaining
When you see `my_string.upper()` in Python, read it as `toupper(my_string)`. Methods let Python chain steps as `object.method().method()`, which plays the same role as R's pipe `|>` (you will also see the older `%>%` from the tidyverse). But not every Python method is chainable: `.append()` above changed the list and returned nothing.
:::

## Libraries

Neither language ships with everything you need for data analysis. **Libraries** (also called packages) add functions for reading data, plotting, and statistics. You load them at the top of your code:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
# library() loads a package and makes all its functions available
library(dplyr)
library(readr)

# Or use a single function without loading the package
dplyr::n_distinct(c(1, 1, 2))
```

## Python

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: true
# import loads a library. as gives it a short nickname
import polars as pl

# Or import a single function
from polars import col
from scipy.stats import ttest_ind
```

:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## R vs Python: using a library's functions
After `library(dplyr)` in R, you call `filter()` directly. After `import polars as pl` in Python, you call `pl.read_csv()` with the nickname in front. Python is explicit about where every function comes from, which avoids two libraries clashing over the same name. The nicknames are conventions everyone uses.

:::

### Tabular data

Most data analysis happens in a dataframe, a table with named columns and one row per observation. The examples use the [Palmer Penguins](https://allisonhorst.github.io/palmerpenguins/) dataset, already loaded in your browser as `penguins.csv`:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
penguins <- read_csv("penguins.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
head(penguins)
```

```{webr}
# Pipe the data through a series of verbs
penguins |>
  filter(!is.na(body_mass_g)) |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarize(
    mean_mass = mean(body_mass_g),
    n = n()
  )
```

## Python

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: true
penguins = pl.read_csv("penguins.csv")
penguins.head()
```

```{pyodide}
# Chain the data through a series of methods
(
    penguins
    .filter(col("body_mass_g").is_not_null())
    .group_by("species")
    .agg(
        mean_mass=col("body_mass_g").mean(),
        n=pl.len(),
    )
)
```

:::

::: {.callout-note}
## dplyr and polars speak the same language
`filter`, `group_by`, and `summarize`/`agg` do the same jobs in both. R pipes with `|>`; Python chains with `.` and wraps the whole chain in parentheses so it can span lines.
:::

### Statistics

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{webr}
two_species <- penguins |>
  filter(species %in% c("Adelie", "Gentoo"))

t.test(body_mass_g ~ species, data = two_species)
```

## Python

```{pyodide}
adelie = penguins.filter(col("species") == "Adelie")["body_mass_g"].drop_nulls()
gentoo = penguins.filter(col("species") == "Gentoo")["body_mass_g"].drop_nulls()

ttest_ind(adelie, gentoo, equal_var=False)
```

:::

## Debugging

An error is the language telling you what went wrong and where. Read an error message from the **bottom up**: the last line names the problem, and the lines above show where it happened. Here are the four you will meet most often:

### Unknown name

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{webr}
#| error: true
mean_score <- 85
print(mean_scroe)
```

## Python

```{pyodide}
#| error: true
mean_score = 85
print(mean_scroe)
```

:::

Almost always a typo, or a variable you have not defined *yet* (did you run the earlier cell?).

### Syntax error

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{webr}
#| error: true
print("hello"
```

## Python

```{pyodide}
#| error: true
print("hello"
```

:::

The language cannot parse what you typed: an unclosed parenthesis or quote, a stray line break, or a missing `:` in Python.

### Wrong type

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{webr}
#| error: true
"76" + 12
```

## Python

```{pyodide}
#| error: true
"76" + 12
```

:::

The operation is fine but the input is the wrong kind of value. Check what you have with `class()` or `type()`.

### Position that does not exist

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{webr}
#| error: true
fruits[10]
```

## Python

```{pyodide}
#| error: true
fruits[10]
```

:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## R vs Python: R is quieter
R returns `NA` for a position that does not exist and keeps going. Python stops with an `IndexError`. Python's habit of stopping early is annoying in the moment but catches mistakes that R would let slip through to your results.
:::

### A 60-second debugging workflow

1. **Read the last line** of the error and name the type of problem out loud.
2. **Check your assumptions** at that line: `class(x)` or `type(x)`, `length(x)` or `len(x)`, the column names of your dataframe.
3. **Shrink the problem**: run just the failing piece on its own. For a broken chain, remove steps from the end until it works, then add them back one at a time.
4. **Change one thing and rerun.** Rerunning is free.
5. Still stuck? **Paste the full error message** into a search engine or AI assistant. The exact wording is what makes errors searchable. See [Working with AI](working-with-ai.qmd) for how to do this well.

## Getting help

Both languages have built-in documentation for every function:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{webr}
# ? or help() opens documentation
?mean
```

## Python

```{pyodide}
# help() prints documentation
help(len)
```

```{pyodide}
# dir() lists every method a value has
dir(my_string)
```

:::
